stories.title: Rural porting war heats up as telcos chase users via richer retailer sops
stories.summary: Bharti Airtel, Reliance Jio, and Vodafone Idea are racing to grab more rural users, riding a fresh wave of port-ins and a sharpened prize hunt as competition heats up
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Telecom operators are ramping up incentives for rural retailers to attract subscribers through Mobile Number Portability (MNP), signalling a shift in the competitive dynamics.

While keeping MNP payouts broadly unchanged, telcos are offering additional incentives equivalent to a month’s recharge or free demo plans for meeting specified port-in targets, according to an IIFL Capital rural survey on telecom trends.
In parts of Rajasthan, retailers received ₹299-349 per MNP after the first five port-ins, effectively equivalent to a free monthly recharge.
In rural Maharashtra, retailers are eligible for a free demo pack from a telco after completing more than three MNPs.
This marks a sharp shift from the research firm’s 2018 rural survey, when operators offered ₹200-210 per port-in only after retailers crossed 50 port-ins.
The new incentives come amid intensifying competition among Bharti Airtel, Reliance Jio and Vodafone Idea (Vi) to expand their subscriber bases, industry sources told businessline.
Vi’s recent move to offer free international roaming on select plans is another sign of the changing competitive landscape, they said.

While the slowdown in incentives had earlier been attributed to the market becoming increasingly duopolistic, industry sources said the renewed push reflects operators’ efforts to protect and grow their subscriber bases.
“Increase in incentives makes sense since the market has become more competitive now that Vodafone Idea is in a better position and can be more aggressive.
The stakes are a little higher.
Almost every operator has an incentive to attract and retain more subscribers,” said Mahesh Uppal, Director, CommFirst (India).

Following the AGR (Adjusted Gross Revenue; a metric used by the DoT to calculate licence fees and spectrum usage charges owed by telecom operator) relief granted to Vi earlier this year, the operator has sought to reinvent itself in the telecom and digital spaces.

stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 05: A mild earthquake measuring 3.2 on the Richter scale struck Pulwama district in Jammu and Kashmir on Monday evening, sending tremors through parts of south and central Kashmir. According to seismic data, the earthquake was recorded at 6:44 pm at a shallow depth of around 5 kilometres. The epicentre was located approximately 28 kilometres southeast of Srinagar, at coordinates 33.890°N latitude and 74.992°E longitude. Given its shallow depth, the tremor was felt in several adjoining areas, particularly across parts of south and central Kashmir. No reports of casualties or damage to property had emerged immediately following the earthquake.

stories.summary: A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant, while declining to entertain the plea filed by advocate Ujjawal Gaur, directed the registry to forward a copy of the petition to all the respondent authorities, asking them to look into the issues raised and take appropriate remedial measures.

article_sentences: A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant, while declining to entertain the plea filed by advocate Ujjawal Gaur, directed the registry to forward a copy of the petition to all the respondent authorities, asking them to look into the issues raised and take appropriate remedial measures.

New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Monday refused to entertain a public interest litigation (PIL) seeking directions to ensure effective measures to prevent recurring floods, riverbank erosion and drainage-related problems in Assam and the Brahmaputra Valley.
Appearing in person, Gaur submitted that the administrative lapses highlighted in the petition were amenable to judicial scrutiny and urged the apex court to issue notice to the authorities.

However, the CJI Kant-led Bench observed that the various suggestions and deficiencies highlighted by the petitioner ought to draw the attention of the concerned authorities, but the issue was "not essentially legal" in nature.
Declining to entertain the PIL, the top court directed its registry to forward the petition to all the respondents, who would look into its contents and take appropriate remedial measures.

The plea had sought judicial intervention to ensure effective implementation of the statutory framework governing flood and erosion management and had proposed, among other measures, a high-level expert mechanism to examine the recurring problems.

The petitioner had contended that the recurring devastation caused by floods could not be treated as wholly inevitable when statutory frameworks and specialised institutions had been created for flood control, bank erosion and drainage management.

The plea referred to the Brahmaputra Board Act, 1980, the Assam Embankment and Drainage Act, 1953 and the River Boards Act, 1956, arguing that these laws contemplated scientific investigation, integrated river-basin planning and implementation of measures relating to floods, erosion and drainage.

It relied on successive reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) which, according to the petitioner, had recorded deficiencies in flood-control planning, execution and maintenance, drainage management, floodplain management and monitoring of projects.

The petition specifically referred to the CAG's Performance Audit on "Flood Control in Assam", contained in Report No. 5 of 2018, which, it claimed, identified deficiencies in integrated basin-wise planning, floodplain zoning, hydrological and morphological studies, execution and monitoring of flood-control works.

It also relied on official records concerning drainage congestion, backflow, inadequate drainage through sluices, encroachment upon natural drainage channels, sedimentation and river morphology as factors aggravating flood vulnerability.

The petitioner further highlighted a shortage of technical manpower in the Brahmaputra Board, referring to an official Lok Sabha reply dated December 12, 2024, which disclosed that 65 of its 182 sanctioned technical posts remained vacant in 2024.

stories.headline: Nepal wraps up Rasuwa flood search; shifts focus to rehabilitation, reconstruction
stories.title: Nepal wraps up Rasuwa flood search; shifts focus to rehabilitation, reconstruction
stories.summary: Kathmandu, Oct 5: Nepal on Monday concluded the search and rescue operation launched after the devastating August 26 flash floods, which claimed at least 1,455 lives, and is now shifting its focus to rehabilitation and reconstruction, officials said. The decision was taken at the 21st meeting of the National Council of the NDRRMA chaired by Prime Minister Balendra Shah at the Singha Durbar Secretariat here, the Prime Minister's Office said. The government decided to wind up the 40-day search and rescue operation, except for essential activities. The meeting directed concerned agencies to expedite rehabilitation and reconstruction works in the areas affected by the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods. "The decision was taken based on recommendations from the District Security Committee, District Disaster Management Committees, the Executive Committee of the NDRRMA, as well as findings from field inspections," it said. The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) has confirmed 1,455 deaths, 5,285 people missing and 13,795 rescued in the disaster.

stories.headline: Did SIR deletions change Tamil Nadu assembly election’s outcome?
stories.title: Did SIR deletions change Tamil Nadu assembly election’s outcome?
stories.summary: While a businessline analysis reveals a striking geographical overlap between high voter removals and TVK victories, experts urge caution against reading it as a conspiracy
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) have stirred protests not just at the national but at the State level too.
In Tamil Nadu, DMK president and former Chief Minister MK Stalin has recently said that the deletion of several lakh voters was one of the reasons for his party’s loss.
The social media is abuzz about how TVK victory may have been aided by these deletions.
A businessline analysis of the granular data on SIR deletions and the outcome of the TN assembly elections in 2026, throws us some interesting trends.
TVK has struggled to win in constituencies where the SIR deletions were lower but has recorded more wins in constituencies where the deletions were higher.
Political analysts and experts however warn that not much should be read into these numbers.
We compared the net reduction in voter count in each constituency as per the April 2026 electoral roll with pre-SIR numbers.
Of the total 234 constituencies, 19 constituencies had lower deletions, of up to 10,000 voters.
In these, the TVK won 2 seats, the DMK 7, the AIADMK 6 and others 4.
Eighty constituencies had deletions between 10,000 to 20,000 voters.
The TVK won 22 of these constituencies, the DMK 20, the AIADMK 24 and others 14.
Sixty-six constituencies had deletions between 20,000 to 30,000.

stories.headline: India-US trade talks hit a plateau as FM flags tough road ahead
stories.title: India-US trade talks hit a plateau as FM flags tough road ahead
stories.summary: India and the United States have reached a “plateau” in their trade negotiations, beyond which further give-and-take would be “very very difficult”, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said at the Munich Security Conference in New Delhi on Monday.“The agreements and negotiations are still ongoing, although we like to believe that both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very very difficult. But maybe if there are rooms to operate from, both sides would do it,” Sitharaman said.Speaking at a session on the next generation of trade agreements, Sitharaman said the talks had been “hard and very rigorously negotiated” but remain unfinalised. She pointed to the core sticking point, which is a trade balance that favours India, leaving Washington keen to narrow the deficit and recover what it sees as past losses.She added that tariffs, once a negotiating instrument within a framework, have been “weaponised”, while countries like India still have to negotiate and trade concessions.“Negotiation used to be the only platform through which countries could highlight the discrepancies, highlight the lopsidedness….Now the imbalance is being sought to be addressed through other means. Tariff was an instrument of negotiation, and tariff had a certain framework within which you will apply it,” the finance minister said.In contrast, she held up the India-EU pact as a model. Covering roughly a quarter of global GDP and trade, India has opened 92.5 percent of tariff lines, about 97 percent by value, while the EU has opened around 99 percent by value. Sensitive sectors, such as dairy and soya for India and meat and dairy for Europe, were carefully managed, she said.Also Read: Nirmala Sitharaman: Global Economy Needs Resilience Amid UncertaintySitharaman argued the deal would boost jobs, as exports such as footwear, textiles, toys and processed components come from labour-intensive micro, small and medium enterprises, employing many women.She also said that bilateral and multilateral deals were never mutually exclusive, but that weakened institutions like the WTO had tilted the balance towards bilateral pacts. “Countries chose where multilateral [agreements] would benefit them, and there are some unique bilaterals which countries choose to have. Now the balance is somewhat built in favour of the bilateral rather than the multilateral,” she added.On the Bilateral Investment Treaty of 2016, she said that India is finalising a new bilateral investment protection template to replace the 2016 model, awaiting cabinet approval.“We had had a template which was cabinet approved in 2016, which itself cancelled out the earlier one, and that became currency….That agreement now we think does not deliver much good for us. So, in the last one and a half years, I worked on a new template for a bilateral protection agreement,” she added. She expects agreements with at least three more countries by December, with Canada likely by December or early next year; Russia is among those in talks.Sitharaman also flagged the strain on food security from fertiliser disruptions. India imports about 80 percent of its requirement, selling a unit to farmers at Rs 300, though it costs Rs 3,000 to import. She said that fertiliser prices have “gone through the roof” while also being a “big challenge” for India since Covid.“Fertilisers have gone through the roof. It is just not possible for any country to sustain buying it at that level,” the minister added. Shipping disruptions and insurance costs after the war in West Asia have prompted a special shipping emergency fund.She said India’s climate commitments continue, citing rooftop solar, solar pumps and new modular nuclear reactor legislation.

stories.headline: Why India's trade policy makes imports cheaper than manufacturing
stories.title: Why India's trade policy makes imports cheaper than manufacturing
stories.summary: In November 2024, a low-carbon ferrochrome (LCFeCr) plant inside the Andhra Pradesh Special Economic Zone (APSEZ) at Atchutapuram near Visakhapatnam fell silent. The SEZ unit, run by TUF Metallurgical Pvt Ltd, had roughly Rs 25 crore invested in it, a dedicated 4,000 KVA power connection, an annual capacity of about 7,200 tonnes, and around 150 workers, directly or indirectly, on its rolls. Its product, LCFeCr, is an alloy used in stainless steel, special alloy steel and foundry applications. While demand for the product persisted, the plant had been priced out of its own supply chain by the government's customs rules.The central issue was how India's trade policy and customs framework determines the duties applicable when a product or mineral is "imported" or "exported" from an Indian SEZ to the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA), or under India's preferential trade agreements (PTAs) with another country. This case highlights inconsistencies embedded in India's trade policy design. It is a story that extends beyond a single plant, company or metal. Similar contradictions could emerge in sectors ranging from chemicals and electronics to textiles.TUF's SEZ unit needed chrome concentrate, its primary raw material, from mines in Odisha for use within another Indian SEZ, an entirely domestic transfer. The fifth proviso to Rule 27(1) of the SEZ Rules purported to require payment of the same 30 percent export duty ordinarily applicable when chrome ore or concentrate is exported from India, even when the material moved from the DTA into an Indian SEZ, on the assumption that any movement into an SEZ qualifies as an "export" for duty purposes.On September 18, 2025, the Andhra Pradesh High Court, in TUF Metallurgical Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (W.P. No. 15528 of 2024), struck down the fifth proviso to Rule 27(1) of the SEZ Rules, 2006, as ultra vires the SEZ Act, 2005. Despite the ruling, consignments already procured from Odisha remained outside the SEZ gate for weeks because customs officials were not informed of the court's decision. The episode highlighted that a legal victory does not automatically guarantee a smooth supply chain.That, however, was only the first challenge.Under Section 30 of the SEZ Act, any finished good that an SEZ unit sells into the rest of India is treated, for customs purposes, as if it were imported from abroad and taxed on its full value, including the labour, power and processing that went into making it.For TUF's ferrochrome, this translates into a customs duty of about 5.5 percent, including the social welfare surcharge. The duty may appear modest until the India-Oman Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), which came into force on June 1, 2026, is taken into account. opening: In November 2024, a low-carbon ferrochrome (LCFeCr) plant inside the Andhra Pradesh Special Economic Zone (APSEZ) at Atchutapuram near Visakhapatnam fell silent.

The SEZ unit, run by TUF Metallurgical Pvt Ltd, had roughly Rs 25 crore invested in it, a dedicated 4,000 KVA power connection, an annual capacity of about 7,200 tonnes, and around 150 workers, directly or indirectly, on its rolls.
body: Its product, LCFeCr, is an alloy used in stainless steel, special alloy steel and foundry applications.
While demand for the product persisted, the plant had been priced out of its own supply chain by the government's customs rules.

The central issue was how India's trade policy and customs framework determines the duties applicable when a product or mineral is "imported" or "exported" from an Indian SEZ to the Domestic Tariff Area (DTA), or under India's preferential trade agreements (PTAs) with another country.
This case highlights inconsistencies embedded in India's trade policy design.
It is a story that extends beyond a single plant, company or metal.
Similar contradictions could emerge in sectors ranging from chemicals and electronics to textiles.
TUF's SEZ unit needed chrome concentrate, its primary raw material, from mines in Odisha for use within another Indian SEZ, an entirely domestic transfer.

The fifth proviso to Rule 27(1) of the SEZ Rules purported to require payment of the same 30 percent export duty ordinarily applicable when chrome ore or concentrate is exported from India, even when the material moved from the DTA into an Indian SEZ, on the assumption that any movement into an SEZ qualifies as an "export" for duty purposes.
On September 18, 2025, the Andhra Pradesh High Court, in TUF Metallurgical Pvt.
Union of India (W.P. No. 15528 of 2024), struck down the fifth proviso to Rule 27(1) of the SEZ Rules, 2006, as ultra vires the SEZ Act, 2005.
Despite the ruling, consignments already procured from Odisha remained outside the SEZ gate for weeks because customs officials were not informed of the court's decision.
The episode highlighted that a legal victory does not automatically guarantee a smooth supply chain.
That, however, was only the first challenge.

Under Section 30 of the SEZ Act, any finished good that an SEZ unit sells into the rest of India is treated, for customs purposes, as if it were imported from abroad and taxed on its full value, including the labour, power and processing that went into making it.
The duty may appear modest until the India-Oman Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), which came into force on June 1, 2026, is taken into account.

Under the CEPA, qualifying LCFeCr manufactured in Oman, including in an Omani free zone where the applicable Rules of Origin are satisfied, can enter India at zero customs duty under tariff item 72024900.
The result is that the Indian manufacturing unit is taxed at both ends of its value chain.
A further competitive asymmetry arises from the fact that Oman's Free Zone allows duty-free import of chrome concentrate, a key raw material for LCFeCr production, from Pakistan.
The material can subsequently be used in ferrochrome manufacturing.
The India-Oman CEPA does not address such inconsistencies.
An Oman-based producer can source duty-free raw materials from Pakistan, while Indian manufacturers face substantially higher import duties.

The issue goes beyond conventional tariff liberalisation and raises questions about the adequacy of the CEPA's Rules of Origin, anti-circumvention provisions and India's domestic tariff structure for critical industrial inputs.

India could address this through stricter product-specific scrutiny of Rules of Origin, closer examination of the economic transformation occurring in Oman under the CEPA framework and, where economically justified, rationalisation of domestic tariffs on chrome concentrate.
The incentive structure is reversed.
The consequences are not merely theoretical.
They raise significant concerns about commercial viability and public interest.
If one considers both factors together, the incentive structure is effectively reversed.
An entrepreneur deciding where to establish the next chrome-alloy furnace may conclude that an Indian SEZ is no longer the most competitive location.
In an Indian SEZ, the finished product is taxed as an import when sold domestically.
In contrast, the same product can be manufactured in a free zone in Oman, such as the Sohar Free Zone, and shipped into India duty-free.

India has, in effect, created a policy architecture in which manufacturing domestically can become more expensive than manufacturing abroad and importing the final product back into the country, a classic inverted duty structure.

This disadvantage may be compounded by fiscal incentives, including corporate tax holidays or exemptions available, subject to applicable conditions, in competing free-zone jurisdictions such as Oman.
With around 150 direct and indirect jobs dependent on the Atchutapuram unit, the case illustrates the practical consequences of this policy dilemma.

Downstream stainless steel and alloy steel manufacturers would likely have preferred sourcing from a nearby Indian supplier, benefiting from shorter lead times and easier technical coordination rather than relying on a longer import chain.
Instead, the outcome has been a loss of employment, capacity utilisation, supplier relationships, tax collections and investor confidence.

It also affects government revenues because an idle plant, power connection and industrial land generate neither GST nor income tax, nor the wider economic activity associated with a functioning factory.
A fix without undoing trade agreements.
These individual policies are not unreasonable in isolation.
Taxing SEZ goods sold into India as imports also has a rationale if the SEZ is legally treated as being outside the customs territory.
Similarly, a zero-duty concession to Oman can be justified as part of a trade agreement that provides reciprocal market access.
The problem is that these policies have not been adequately evaluated in combination.

As the TUF case demonstrates, their cumulative effect is to create an incentive to relocate manufacturing activity that India is fully capable of undertaking domestically, contrary to the objectives of Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat.
The policy solution does not require dismantling the Oman CEPA or other PTAs, abandoning the export-oriented character of SEZs, or providing ferrochrome producers with permanent subsidies.
Rather, it requires a narrower and more targeted approach.
SEZ units selling into India should pay customs duty only on the duty foregone on imported inputs, rather than on the value added through domestic labour, power and manufacturing processes.

India already follows this principle under two comparable schemes: Export Oriented Undertakings (EOUs) and the MOOWR scheme (Manufacturing and Other Operations in Warehouse), which allows manufacturers to import raw materials and capital goods without paying customs duty upfront.
In both cases, the customs duty foregone on imported inputs is recovered when goods are sold domestically, instead of taxing the finished product as a notional import.
There appears to be no significant administrative obstacle to extending the same principle to SEZ clearances into the DTA.

The government has already taken a limited and temporary step in this direction by introducing a concessional-duty window for eligible SEZ-to-DTA clearances between April 1, 2026 and March 31, 2027 through Notification No. 11/2026-Customs dated March 31, 2026.
However, TUF's Low Carbon Ferro Chrome, classified under tariff item 72024900, does not appear to be covered by the notification.
More fundamentally, the March 2026 notification could be viewed as an acknowledgement that the existing SEZ-to-DTA duty framework may require corrective intervention in certain circumstances.
A more durable solution would be to incorporate a duty-recovery mechanism directly into the SEZ Act for all eligible products rather than relying on ad hoc exemptions.
Such an approach would provide the predictability required in a competitive trading environment.
Ensuring a level playing field.

A more fundamental intervention would ensure that products manufactured in Indian SEZs receive treatment comparable to products imported under India's PTAs when they enter the DTA, subject to appropriate safeguards.
This would create a level playing field for domestic manufacturing.
Indian SEZ-produced goods should not face higher duties when entering the DTA than identical or comparable products manufactured abroad and imported under a PTA.

Such an approach would strengthen the competitiveness of India's manufacturing base and support the objectives of Make in India, while preserving the integrity of the SEZ framework and India's preferential trade commitments.
India is negotiating and signing free trade and preferential trade agreements at a faster pace than at any point in its history.
Yet tariff concessions are being layered onto an existing framework of domestic exemptions, SEZ regulations and customs rules.
The combined effect of new concessions and existing regulations requires much closer scrutiny before future agreements are concluded.

For manufacturing growth and investor confidence, one question should be asked consistently: Do newly negotiated tariff concessions, when combined with existing rules, make it cheaper to import a finished product than to manufacture it in India or an Indian SEZ?
Where the answer is yes, as it currently is for ferrochrome, the issue is worth fixing before the furnace goes cold, not after.

stories.headline: Samvidhaan Pe Charcha 4.0 at Parul University Connects Constitutional Thought with Contemporary Legal Practice
stories.title: Samvidhaan Pe Charcha 4.0 at Parul University Connects Constitutional Thought with Contemporary Legal Practice
stories.summary: Parul University held the fourth edition of its flagship legal conclave, Samvidhaan Pe Charcha 4.0. The event was attended by eminent members of the judiciary, senior advocates, legal professionals and law students for a series of discussions on constitutional values, contemporary legal questions and the changing landscape of law. The conclave had expert addresses, interactive sessions, PU Talks, workshops and competitive platforms, giving students an opportunity to interact with the legal fraternity beyond the classroom. The proceedings featured Hon’ble Mr. Justice Vipul M. Pancholi , Judge, Supreme Court of India, Hon’ble Mr. Justice D.N. Ray , Judge, High Court of Gujarat, Hon’ble Mr. Justice N.S. Sanjay Gowda , Judge, High Court of Gujarat, Shri Gaurav Bhatia , Senior Advocate, Supreme Court of India and National Spokesperson, BJP, Ms. Mahalakshmi Pavani , Senior Advocate, Supreme Court of India, and Ms. Anitha Shenoy , Senior Advocate, Supreme Court of India, alongside other distinguished members of the legal fraternity. Their presence provided an opportunity for aspirant lawyers to hear first hand the views of the judiciary and to learn about the practical aspects of legal education and advocacy. Reflecting on the relevance of constitutional principles to the legal profession and spotlighting the future lawyers, Hon’ble Mr. Justice Vipul Manubhai Pancholi said , “A law school has a responsibility not merely to impart legal knowledge but also to nurture professional ethics, constitutional values and social responsibility. Therefore, the lawyer of the future must not only know the law but also understand the society and technology within which the law operates. As future advocates, remember that advocacy is not merely about winning but about assisting the court in reaching a just and legally sound conclusion.” Addressing the audience, Hon’ble Mr. Justice D.N. Ray shared his perspective on constitutional and legal issues along with his thoughts on how today's youth is facing the challenges that come with the fast growing world. He said “ In this age of instant gratification and instant success, please be prepared to fail, which is the most important lesson which nobody will ever tell you. It is okay to fail. There's no problem. So the most important thing is to fail and to live on with all these experiences and to understand that there is no competition which you are actually fighting. Your only competitor is You yourself.” The proceedings also included an interactive engagement followed by aPU Talk by Shri Gaurav Bhatia, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court of India and National Spokesperson, BJP on “The Living Constitution: Democracy, Rule of Law & Changing Landscape of Fundamental Rights” . This session discussed the relevance of the constitutional principles and the changing understanding of the basic rights in contemporary India. Bringing the discourse closer to the present constitutional scenario and emphasizing the need to understand constitutional principles within the framework of an evolving society, he said “ The Constitution is a document which talks about equality, liberty, fraternity, justice. What is the purpose of life if you can't be treated with dignity? More important than even existence. Life is not about breathing. Life is about adding soul to your lifespan, and dignity is that soul.” Talking to the students on the topic of the Indian Constitution then, now, and tomorrow , Hon’ble Mr. Justice N.S. Sanjay Gowda , Judge, High Court of Gujarat, said “ A constitution is a document which basically creates us. The basic requirement of the constitution is not to tell us what we can do, but what we cannot and we should not do.” On the occasion, Dr.Devanshu Patel, President, Parul University said, “Samvidhaan Pe Charcha is an endeavor to bring constitutional thought into meaningful dialogue with the next generation of legal professionals. By meeting judges, advocates and experts, students gain perspectives that complement their academic learning and that motivate them to take a more active interest in the principles, responsibilities and realities of the legal profession.” The conclave also acknowledged the performance of law students of Parul University in various prestigious national competitions. Sachidanand Patil, Jay Gawalni and Ishant Suthar, winners of 11th Shri N. J. Yasaswy Memorial Moot Court Competition 2026 hosted by ICFAI Law School, Hyderabad were congratulated along with Priyodarshini Roy, Best Speaker at National Moot Court Competition 2026 organised by Innovation Institute of Law, New Delhi. Kunj Prajapati also received a Special Mention at the largest debate conference of JG University, Gujarat and Swayam Prakash Shukla won a Bronze Verbal Mention in AIPPM . Moot Court Competition was the continuation of the competitive proceedings of Samvidhaan Pe Charcha 4.0, with Quarter Final and Semi-Final rounds being held in English and Gujarati, offering a practical platform for students to put their legal research, argumentation and advocacy skills into practice in front of experienced legal professionals. The academic program also featured workshops on “Innovation Vs. Regulation: Finding the Constitutional Balance in the Digital Economy” by Mr. Nihit Nagpal and “Samvidhan or Adhikar: Equality, Liberty & Dignity in Contemporary India” by Mr. Zafar Khurshid . The competitions in English and Gujarati provided students with a chance to put their legal reasoning and advocacy skills to the test in a competitive environment. The three-day conclave concluded with addresses by senior members of the judiciary, an interactive session of Q&A with students and the felicitation and prize distribution of participants. Hon’ble Mr. Justice Surendra Pandey, Judge, Patna High Court , spoke on constitutional values, human dignity and judicial responsibility and asked students to think about litigation and contribute to the justice-delivery system. He reminded them, adding “ You don't have to become enemies only because the other person has a different point of view,” and added “The judges do not own the constitution. they have just been given the duty to interpret it. It's owned by all of us.” Justice Soman Sen, Chief Justice, Kerala High Court , shared his views on Fundamental Rights, Article 21, constitutional morality, the Emergency, basic structure and challenges presented by new technologies . He said, “We may leave this auditorium today, but the constitution cannot remain inside it.” He also stressed the importance of thought and reasoning in legal advocacy: “The strength of an argument does not come from the volume in which it is delivered, but from the quality of thought behind it.” Speaking about the career paths of young lawyers, Justice N. Koteshwar Singh, Judge, Supreme Court of India , advised the students to look into the emerging areas like AI, cybercrime, forensic science and patents and also advised them not to make money their first priority. “Don't think of money when you start,” he said and stressed “The most important is the dignity of the individuals. That is the core.” His advice to the students was simple: “Be a smart lawyer.” Students asked questions on regional diversity in the judiciary, social media algorithms, delays in criminal trials, religious and civil disputes, prolonged incarceration, NDPS cases and the right to speedy trial during the last interaction. The event culminated with the prize distribution of 3rd State Moot Court Competition (Gujarati) and 4th Inter-University Moot Court Competition 2026 with the prize money of Rs 15,000 to Rs 60,000 in the former and Rs 40,000 to Rs 1.75 lakh in the latter. Samvidhaan Pe Charcha 4.0 united judicial wisdom, professional perspectives and student advocacy, providing law students with a platform to engage with the Constitution, contemporary legal questions and the realities of the justice system through dialog, competition and direct interaction with leading legal minds. article_sentences: Underlining the need to take preventive measures against sexual offences, the Supreme Court on Monday (October 5, 2026) asked the Delhi.
Police to set up 24-hour monitoring cells for continuous surveillance of vulnerable areas.
The court also asked the police to strengthen patrolling, particularly around educational institutions and public spaces.

A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran observed that the mere installation of CCTV cameras in public spaces would serve little purpose without continuous monitoring to detect suspicious activity and enable a swift police response.
“When we are talking about surveillance through CCTV cameras, how far will they help curb crimes if there is no continuous monitoring at different war rooms?
The cameras will help you in catching hold of the culprit, but how will you prevent such crimes?
There has to be a cell — a 24-hour cell — which keeps monitoring what is happening,” the Bench observed.
The court was hearing a suo motu case concerning a spate of sexual assault incidents involving minors and women in the Delhi-National Capital Region.

On September 28, the Supreme Court Collegium had recommended elevation of Justice Sunita Agarwal (Chief Justice of Gujarat High Court), Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya (Chief Justice of Delhi High Court) and Justice Aparesh Kumar Singh (Chief Justice of Telangana High Court).

He was appointed as the Chief Standing Counsel, State of U.P. in May 2007 and continued to hold that office till elevation as a Judge.
He took oath as a permanent Judge of the High Court on August 6 2013.

State of West Bengal.

It further seeks publication of annual reports on SHRC websites and in the public domain, alongwith their placement before the respective state legislatures.

article_sentences: While speaking at her farewell reference on Monday (October 5), Gujarat High Court Chief Justice Sunita Agarwal asked women lawyers in the profession not to let circumstances, expectations and doubts of others to determine the limits of their achievements.
The Chief Justice asked the women lawyers in the profession who are already established to hold the hands of those female bar members who are climbing up as well as guide them in the profession.
Notably, the Central government today notified Justice Agarwal's elevation to the Supreme Court.
"And to the young women in the profession, you are the foremost in my mind in a lot of what I do.
My goal is to make this institution a beautiful place for you where you can find yourself and achieve whatever you seek and deserve.
Do not allow circumstances, expectations and doubts of others to determine the limits of your achievements.
In my career I have met the same obstacles as you.
And it was perseverance which carried me through.

To the women already established in the profession, on the bench or at the bar, whichever rung of the professional ladder you stand on today, hold the hands of those who are climbing up, guide them, nurture them and give them the confidence to persevere".
At the outset, Justice Agarwal said that she finds it difficult to leave the High Court which over the years had assumed immense significance in her life.
"Last 3 years have been a turning point for my professional and personal growth…these years taught me to keep going despite the difficulties around me.
To stay grounded and to keep working without losing my grit," the judge said.
